rationale: A wins because it knows where the floor is. Its angle "Substack says its top creators made over $400M last year - but won't say who or how much each" turns the strongest fact into a reporter-shaped scrutiny story without decorating it. B has more swagger, but "YouTube runs on ads. Substack's video play bets that creators would rather own their audience" imports a competitor war and audience-ownership thesis the update did not supply. That is how a founder gets talked into a pitch that collapses on the first fact-check.
gaps_in_A: "short on funding" overstates the supplied fact; the update says only "public funding struggles," not a current cash position.
"capital-intensive infrastructure" may be true, but it is an inference; the update gives no cost, hosting architecture, or vendor detail.
"the same cut now extending over video and podcast monetization" gets ahead of the facts; the set later asks whether the cut applies, but the angle copy states it too firmly.
gaps_in_B: "YouTube runs on ads" imports YouTube, ads, and a platform-comparison frame that was not in the update.
"subscription fatigue narrative" and "widely published since 2022-2023" is a manufactured external peg unless separately sourced.
"implying $40M or more flowed to Substack" does math on an undefined $400M claim; no proof says that figure is gross subscription revenue subject to the 10% cut.
"a specific writer with 10,000 paid subscribers" invents a customer profile and scale. Cute example, bad discipline.
